subject: Chemistry
title: How Atoms Hold Hands: Bonding & Shapes
hook: Why does water form a V-shape? Why is ice less dense than liquid water? The answer lies in how atoms bond.

slides.title: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel holds up two beakers: one with salt (ionic), one with sugar (covalent). 'Same carbon atoms inside both, yet one dissolves instantly, the other resists. Why?'

image.alt: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Why Do Atoms Bond?
slides.storyContext: Atoms bond to achieve lower energy. Most stable configuration: filled valence shells (octet rule). Atoms will give, take, or share electrons to reach this stability. Different strategies = different bond types.

image.alt: Why Do Atoms Bond? — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Priya's Kitchen Discovery
slides.storyContext: Priya notices salt crystals dissolve instantly in water while sugar takes longer to stir. Dr. Patel explains: 'Salt breaks apart into ions immediately—electrostatic repulsion in water is too strong. Sugar stays whole—the C-C and C-O bonds are covalent, held tight.'

image.alt: Priya's Kitchen Discovery — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Ionic Bonding: Complete Electron Transfer

points.label: Definition
points.text: Metal GIVES electrons to nonmetal. Electrostatic attraction between cation and anion.

points.label: Example: NaCl
points.text: Na (1 valence e⁻) → gives to Cl (7 valence e⁻). Na⁺ and Cl⁻ attract strongly.

points.label: Properties
points.text: Crystalline solids, high melting point, conduct in molten state or aqueous solution, brittle.

example.problem: Write the electron transfer for MgO formation.
example.solution: Mg (2 e⁻) → transfers both to O (6 e⁻). Mg²⁺ + O²⁻ → MgO. Both now have stable octets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ionic bonds form when one atom completely gives electrons to another, creating charged ions that attract each other—like a magnet.

image.alt: Ionic Bonding: Complete Electron Transfer — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Ionic vs. Covalent: Salt vs. Sugar
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Both salt and sugar contain positive and negative charges. Why does salt dissolve instantly but sugar needs stirring?' The answer: how the electrons are held.

example.problem: NaCl (salt) vs. C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ (sugar): both have charged regions. Why does NaCl dissolve 100x faster?
example.solution: NaCl is ionic: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are separate ions held by electrostatic force. Water molecules (polar) surround each ion, breaking the crystal. Sugar is covalent: C, H, O atoms share electrons in a tightly bonded molecule. Water can't separate the atoms—it must dissolve the whole molecule intact, which is slower.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ionic crystals break apart into individual ions, which dissolve instantly. Covalent molecules stay bonded together and dissolve more slowly.

image.alt: Ionic vs. Covalent: Salt vs. Sugar — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Covalent Bonding: Electron Sharing

points.label: Definition
points.text: Atoms SHARE electrons in orbitals. Both atoms benefit from the shared pair.

points.label: Single, double, triple bonds
points.text: C-H: 1 pair (single), O=O: 2 pairs (double), N≡N: 3 pairs (triple).

points.label: Polar vs. nonpolar
points.text: Nonpolar: equal sharing (Cl-Cl, C-C). Polar: unequal sharing (H-Cl, C-O)—atom with higher electronegativity pulls more.

example.problem: Draw Lewis structure of CO₂. Are there any lone pairs?
example.solution: C is central (less electronegative), O atoms on either side. O=C=O. C has NO lone pairs (4 bonds). Each O has 2 lone pairs (total 4 electrons not bonding).

slides.inSimpleWords: Covalent bonds are atoms sharing electrons to fill their shells. Shared electrons spend more time near the more electronegative atom (polar).

image.alt: Covalent Bonding: Electron Sharing — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: The Oxygen Atom's Greed
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel tells a story: 'Imagine carbon and oxygen sharing a pair of electrons. But oxygen is greedy—it has more positive charge in its nucleus. The shared electrons spend more time circling oxygen than carbon. Result? The oxygen end becomes slightly negative, carbon slightly positive. Polar bond!'

image.alt: The Oxygen Atom's Greed — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Electronegativity & Bond Polarity

points.label: Electronegativity
points.text: Measure of atom's ability to attract electrons. Scale: F (most, 4.0) to Fr (least, 0.7). Increases across period, decreases down group.

points.label: Bond polarity
points.text: ΔEN between atoms determines polarity. ΔEN > 1.7: ionic. 0.4–1.7: polar covalent. <0.4: nonpolar.

points.label: Dipole moment
points.text: Measure of bond polarity. Polar bonds have partial positive (δ+) and negative (δ–) charges.

example.problem: Rank bond polarity: H-H, H-Cl, Cl-Cl. Use electronegativity values.
example.solution: H-H: ΔEN ≈ 0 (nonpolar). Cl-Cl: ΔEN ≈ 0 (nonpolar). H-Cl: ΔEN ≈ 0.9 (polar). Order: H-Cl > H-H = Cl-Cl.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electronegativity measures 'pull' for electrons. Large differences create polar bonds (one end positive, one negative).

slides.title: Lewis Structures & Formal Charge

points.label: Octet rule
points.text: Atoms aim for 8 valence electrons (except H: 2)

points.label: Formal charge
points.text: FC = valence e⁻ - (lone pairs + ½ bonding e⁻). Minimize formal charges.

points.label: Example: Sulfur in H₂SO₄
points.text: S can expand octet (d-orbitals available), holding up to 12 e⁻ (6 bonds).

example.problem: Draw resonance structures for NO₃⁻ (nitrate ion).
example.solution: N is central (5 e⁻ + 1 from charge = 6). Forms 3 bonds with O atoms. One N=O (double), two N-O (single) with negative on the single-bonded O. Three resonance forms: the double bond rotates.

slides.inSimpleWords: Lewis structures show where electrons are. Formal charge helps us pick the most realistic structure when multiple arrangements are possible.

image.alt: Lewis Structures & Formal Charge — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Drawing Lewis Structures Step-by-Step
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel walks Priya through drawing the Lewis structure of ammonia (NH₃) as if solving a puzzle.

example.problem: Draw the Lewis structure of NH₃ (ammonia). Count valence e⁻, show bonds and lone pairs.
example.solution: N has 5 valence e⁻. Each H contributes 1. Total = 8 e⁻. N forms 3 N-H bonds (6 e⁻) + 1 lone pair on N (2 e⁻). Structure: H-N-H with H below and one lone pair above.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count the total valence electrons. Connect atoms with bonds. Place remaining electrons as lone pairs. Goal: 8 e⁻ around each atom (octet).

image.alt: Drawing Lewis Structures Step-by-Step — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Why Resonance Structures Matter
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'If NO₃⁻ has resonance structures, which one is real?' Dr. Patel smiles: 'None—and all. Reality is a blend of all three. The actual N-O bond is between single and double. Resonance is a limitation of Lewis structures; reality is more nuanced.'

slides.title: Valence Bond Theory & Hybridization

points.label: Overlap
points.text: Bonds form when atomic orbitals overlap. More overlap = stronger bond.

points.label: Hybridization
points.text: Mixing of orbitals to match molecular geometry. sp (linear), sp² (trigonal), sp³ (tetrahedral).

points.label: Example: Methane CH₄
points.text: C: 1s² 2s² 2p². Hybridizes to sp³ (4 equal orbitals), forming 4 identical C-H bonds at 109.5° angles.

example.problem: Ethene (C₂H₄): What is the hybridization of each carbon?
example.solution: Each C forms 3 bonds (2 C-H + 1 C=C). sp² hybridization. The C=C is σ + π bond. Bond angle ≈ 120°.

slides.inSimpleWords: Atoms can reshape their orbitals (hybridize) to match the shape of the molecule they're forming. This explains why bonds are arranged the way they are.

image.alt: Valence Bond Theory & Hybridization — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Why Methane is Tetrahedral
slides.storyContext: Arjun wonders: 'Carbon has p-orbitals which are dumbbell-shaped. But methane's bonds all look the same, equally spaced. How can that be?' Dr. Patel explains hybridization: carbon mixes its s and p orbitals into 4 identical hybrid orbitals, pointing toward the 4 corners of a tetrahedron.

image.alt: Why Methane is Tetrahedral — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Sigma & Pi Bonds

points.label: Sigma (σ) bonds
points.text: Head-on orbital overlap, cylindrical symmetry. Strongest. Found in all single bonds; one per bond.

points.label: Pi (π) bonds
points.text: Sideways orbital overlap (p-orbitals). Weaker. Found in double and triple bonds (1 π per double, 2 π per triple).

points.label: Double bond example
points.text: C=C is 1 σ (strong, rigid) + 1 π (allows no rotation). Triple N≡N is 1 σ + 2 π.

example.problem: Why can't C=C rotate, but C-C can?
example.solution: C-C is 1 σ bond (cylindrical)—rotation around the axis doesn't break it. C=C adds a π bond (above/below plane)—rotation would break the π overlap. Rigid.

slides.inSimpleWords: σ bonds are strong, rotatable (single bonds). π bonds restrict rotation and are found in double/triple bonds. This is why double bonds have fixed geometry.

slides.title: VSEPR Theory: Predicting Molecular Shape

points.label: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion)
points.text: Electron pairs (bonding + lone) repel each other. They arrange to maximize distance.

points.label: Geometry from electron pairs
points.text: 2 pairs: linear. 3: trigonal planar. 4: tetrahedral. 5: trigonal bipyramidal. 6: octahedral.

points.label: Molecular shape
points.text: Ignore lone pairs for the final shape name, but they affect bond angles.

example.problem: What is the shape of NH₃ (ammonia)?
example.solution: N (5 e⁻) + 3 H (1 e⁻ each) = 8 e⁻ total = 4 electron pairs. One lone pair on N. Electron geometry: tetrahedral. Molecular shape: trigonal pyramidal (pyramid, not flat). Bond angle < 109.5° due to lone-pair repulsion.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electron pairs push away from each other, spreading out as far as possible. This decides the shape of the molecule—V-shaped water, tetrahedral methane, etc.

image.alt: VSEPR Theory: Predicting Molecular Shape — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: VSEPR Practice: Water's V-Shape
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel holds up a model of water (H-O-H). 'Why is it V-shaped, not linear? Let's count the electron pairs.'

example.problem: Water (H₂O): predict the shape using VSEPR. O has 6 valence e⁻.
example.solution: O: 6 e⁻. Forms 2 O-H bonds (4 e⁻ shared) + 2 lone pairs (4 e⁻). Total: 4 electron pairs. Electron geometry: tetrahedral. Molecular shape: BENT (or V-shaped). Bond angle: ~104.5° (less than 109.5° due to lone-pair repulsion).

slides.inSimpleWords: Water isn't linear because oxygen has TWO lone pairs. The 4 electron pairs arrange tetrahedrally, leaving the 2 H atoms at a V-angle.

image.alt: VSEPR Practice: Water's V-Shape — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Lone Pairs as Invisible Players
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'If lone pairs aren't part of the molecular shape, why do they matter?' Dr. Patel explains: 'Lone pairs take up space and repel bonds harder than bonds repel each other. So they squish bond angles smaller. That's why water (2 lone pairs) is 104.5°, not 109.5°. The lone pairs are invisible players, but they're choreographing the dance.'

slides.title: Hydrogen Bonding & Intermolecular Forces

points.label: Hydrogen bond
points.text: Special case of polar covalent bonding. H bonded to F, O, or N acts as partial positive; lone pair on F/O/N is attracted.

points.label: Strength order
points.text: Ionic > Hydrogen bond > Dipole-dipole > London forces (weakest)

points.label: Example: Water
points.text: H-O-H. Partial positive H on one molecule attracts lone pair on O of another. Creates hydrogen-bonded network—explains high boiling point (100°C vs NH₃ at -33°C).

example.problem: Why does ice float? (Hint: Hydrogen bonding in solid water.)
example.solution: In ice, hydrogen bonds form a crystalline lattice with LARGE gaps. Density of ice < liquid water. When you melt it, the structure collapses, and density increases—unique property.

slides.inSimpleWords: Hydrogen bonds (partial ionic attraction) are strong compared to other non-covalent forces. They're why water boils at 100°C instead of ~50°C, and why life exists.

image.alt: Hydrogen Bonding & Intermolecular Forces — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Why Ice Floats (A True Rarity)
slides.storyContext: Priya learns that ice is less dense than liquid water—the only common substance with this property. Dr. Patel explains: 'Hydrogen bonds in ice spread molecules far apart. In liquid water, they're closer, so liquid is denser. This is why ice floats, why lakes freeze from the top, why fish survive beneath the ice.'

image.alt: Why Ice Floats (A True Rarity) — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Worked Problem: Molecular Geometry & Polarity
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel asks: 'CF₄ and CHF₃ both contain C-F bonds. But one is polar and one isn't. Which, and why?'

example.problem: CF₄ (carbon tetrafluoride) vs CHF₃ (fluoroform): predict shape and polarity.
example.solution: CF₄: C with 4 F. Tetrahedral, symmetric → all dipoles cancel → NONPOLAR. CHF₃: C with 3 F + 1 H. Also tetrahedral, but asymmetric (H less electronegative than F) → dipoles DON'T cancel → POLAR.

slides.inSimpleWords: A molecule's polarity depends on both bond polarity AND shape. Symmetrical molecules can be nonpolar even if bonds are polar.

image.alt: Worked Problem: Molecular Geometry & Polarity — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Polarity Challenge: CO₂ vs H₂O
slides.storyContext: Arjun observes: 'Both CO₂ and H₂O contain polar bonds (C-O and H-O). Yet CO₂ doesn't dissolve well in water, while H₂O mixes with itself. Why?'

example.problem: CO₂ (linear: O=C=O) vs H₂O (bent): both have polar bonds, but one is polar overall and one isn't. Explain.
example.solution: CO₂: linear and symmetric. Dipoles point LEFT (from C toward left O) and RIGHT (from C toward right O). They cancel → NONPOLAR molecule. H₂O: bent shape. Dipoles point from H toward O. They don't cancel; resultant points perpendicular to H-H line → POLAR molecule. Polar water dissolves polar solutes and H-bonds; nonpolar CO₂ cannot.

slides.inSimpleWords: Linear, symmetrical molecules cancel dipoles (nonpolar). Bent or asymmetric molecules don't (polar). Shape is everything for polarity.

image.alt: Polarity Challenge: CO₂ vs H₂O — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Why 'Like Dissolves Like'
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Why does oil not mix with water?' Dr. Patel explains: 'Oil is nonpolar—C-C and C-H bonds with little to no dipole. Water is highly polar. Polar molecules hydrogen-bond with each other; nonpolar molecules don't. They're incompatible. 'Like dissolves like' means polar solvents dissolve polar solutes, nonpolar dissolves nonpolar.'

slides.title: Your Turn: Design a Molecule
slides.storyContext: Arjun challenges Priya: 'If you want to design a molecule with a strong hydrogen bond, what should you include?'

example.problem: Design a molecule with strong hydrogen bonding. List requirements.
example.solution: Must contain: (1) H bonded to F, O, or N (to create partial positive), (2) F, O, or N with lone pairs to accept the hydrogen bond. Example: ethanol (C₂H₅OH) has O-H group → strong hydrogen bonding. This is why alcohols have high boiling points.

image.alt: Your Turn: Design a Molecule — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Challenge: Predicting Boiling Points
slides.storyContext: Priya notices that ethanol (C₂H₅OH) boils at 78°C, while dimethyl ether (CH₃OCH₃) boils at -25°C, even though they have the same molecular formula! What's the difference?

example.problem: Ethanol vs dimethyl ether: same molecular formula C₂H₆O, but different structures and boiling points. Why?
example.solution: Ethanol: has O-H group → hydrogen bonding between molecules → strong intermolecular forces → HIGH boiling point (78°C). Dimethyl ether: O is in the middle (CH₃-O-CH₃) → no H-O bond → only dipole-dipole forces → LOW boiling point (-25°C). Hydrogen bonding > dipole-dipole forces.

image.alt: Challenge: Predicting Boiling Points — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

slides.title: Putting It All Together: A Molecule's Biography
slides.storyContext: Dr. Patel summarizes: 'Every molecule has a biography. First, atoms choose a bonding strategy (ionic or covalent). Then, the electrons arrange themselves (Lewis structure, resonance). Then, orbitals hybridize to match the geometry (sp, sp², sp³). Finally, lone pairs adjust the angles (VSEPR). Last, molecules interact via hydrogen bonds. All of this determines whether a substance is a crystal, a gas, or alive.'

slides.title: Bonding & Structure Essentials

points.text: Ionic: complete electron transfer (high melting point, brittle)
Covalent: electron sharing (variable properties)
Lewis structures show valence electrons; formal charge picks the best structure
Hybridization (sp, sp², sp³) matches bonding geometry
VSEPR predicts shape: electron pairs repel, maximize distance
Hydrogen bonds (H to F/O/N) are strong intermolecular forces—explain water's unique properties

slides.inSimpleWords: Chemical bonds hold atoms together. The type of bond (ionic, covalent, hydrogen bond) and the shape of the molecule determine all its properties.

image.alt: Bonding & Structure Essentials — Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

subject: Chemistry
title: Energy & Thermodynamics: Heat, Work & Why Reactions Happen
hook: Why does a candle flame release heat but never needs external energy? Understanding energy changes reveals the why.

slides.title: Thermodynamics
slides.storyContext: Dr. Singh lights a candle in class. 'This flame is just a chemical reaction releasing energy. But what IS energy? Where does it go? Why MUST the reaction happen?'

image.alt: Thermodynamics — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Energy in Chemistry
slides.storyContext: Every reaction moves energy around. Breaking bonds costs energy (endothermic). Forming bonds releases energy (exothermic). The NET change decides if a reaction is spontaneous. This is thermodynamics.

image.alt: Energy in Chemistry — Thermodynamics

slides.title: The Candle Never Stops Burning (Until Fuel Runs Out)
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'If burning candle wax releases energy, why doesn't the whole thing explode at once?' Dr. Singh explains: 'Breaking wax bonds costs energy (endothermic). Forming CO₂ and H₂O bonds releases MORE energy (exothermic). The flame itself is where this battle is happening—heat from products breaks more reactant bonds. A cascade.'

image.alt: The Candle Never Stops Burning (Until Fuel Runs Out) — Thermodynamics

slides.title: System, Surroundings, Universe

points.label: System
points.text: The reaction or process we're studying (inside a beaker, inside a cell)

points.label: Surroundings
points.text: Everything else (the room, the air, Earth)

points.label: Universe
points.text: System + Surroundings. Total energy is conserved (First Law).

example.problem: When you burn sugar (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O), identify the system.
example.solution: System = the sugar + oxygen inside the container. Surroundings = the container, room air, everything outside the beaker. The heat released goes TO the surroundings.

slides.inSimpleWords: Think of thermodynamics as energy accounting. The system is what we're studying. The surroundings are everything else. Energy moves between them but is never lost.

image.alt: System, Surroundings, Universe — Thermodynamics

slides.title: System vs. Surroundings in Your Kitchen
slides.storyContext: Priya boils water in a kettle. She asks Dr. Singh: 'Where is the system here? The water? The kettle? The stove?'

example.problem: In a boiling kettle: where is the system? What are the surroundings?
example.solution: System = the water inside the kettle (what we're studying—liquid becoming gas). Surroundings = the kettle metal, the stove burner, the air in the kitchen, everything else. Heat flows from the stove (surroundings) into the water (system) to make it boil.

slides.inSimpleWords: Define the system first: it's whatever process you care about. Everything else is surroundings. Energy flows between them.

image.alt: System vs. Surroundings in Your Kitchen — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Heat, Work & Internal Energy

points.label: Internal Energy (U)
points.text: Total kinetic + potential energy of all particles in the system

points.label: Heat (q)
points.text: Energy transfer due to temperature difference. +q = energy in (endothermic), -q = energy out (exothermic)

points.label: Work (w)
points.text: Energy transfer due to force × distance. Common: PV work when gas expands (w = -PΔV)

example.problem: A gas expands against 1 atm pressure, increasing volume by 2 L. Calculate work.
example.solution: w = -PΔV = -(1 atm)(2 L) = -2 L·atm. Convert: -2 × 101.3 = -202.6 J. Negative = work done BY system ON surroundings.

slides.inSimpleWords: Internal energy is the total energy stored in a substance (heat of atoms moving). Heat is energy transfer due to temperature. Work is energy from pushing against resistance.

image.alt: Heat, Work & Internal Energy — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Heat vs. Work: Two Ways to Transfer Energy
slides.storyContext: Dr. Singh demonstrates: 'I can warm this beaker two ways. (1) Put it on a hot plate—heat flows through the metal (thermal transfer). (2) Squeeze it in a tire pump—friction heats it up (work). Both raise internal energy. The system doesn't care HOW energy arrives, only that it does.'

image.alt: Heat vs. Work: Two Ways to Transfer Energy — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Why Work Matters in Real Reactions
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'In chemistry, why does work matter? Don't we just care about heat?' Dr. Singh nods: 'Good question. In a rigid container, NO work—all energy goes to internal energy. But in your car engine, a gas expands, pushing the piston. That's PV work—it's how cars move. Work and heat are equally real.'

slides.title: First Law of Thermodynamics

points.label: Statement
points.text: ΔU = q + w. Change in internal energy = heat + work.

points.label: Conservation
points.text: Energy is never created or destroyed, only transformed.

points.label: Sign convention
points.text: +q: heat absorbed (endothermic), -q: heat released (exothermic), -w: work done by system (expansion)

example.problem: A reaction absorbs 50 J of heat and 20 J of work is done ON the system. Find ΔU.
example.solution: ΔU = q + w = (+50 J) + (+20 J) = +70 J. Internal energy increases by 70 J.

slides.inSimpleWords: The first law says energy is conserved. It can't appear or disappear. A change in internal energy comes from heat and work—nothing else.

image.alt: First Law of Thermodynamics — Thermodynamics

slides.title: First Law in Action: Heating Gas in a Cylinder
slides.storyContext: Priya watches Dr. Singh place a piston-cylinder on a Bunsen burner. 'Heat flows in, the piston rises—gas expands. What's happening to internal energy?'

example.problem: Gas in a cylinder with a piston: 100 J of heat flows in, and the gas does 30 J of work pushing the piston up. Find ΔU.
example.solution: q = +100 J (heat in). w = -30 J (work done BY gas, negative). ΔU = q + w = 100 + (-30) = +70 J. Internal energy increases by 70 J. Some heat went to internal energy, some to lifting the piston.

slides.inSimpleWords: Heat from the flame goes partly into warming the gas (internal energy) and partly into pushing the piston (work). First law divides the incoming heat.

image.alt: First Law in Action: Heating Gas in a Cylinder — Thermodynamics

slides.title: What 'Constant Volume' Really Means
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'If the piston is fixed—doesn't expand—does the First Law change?' Dr. Singh explains: 'At constant volume, the gas can't do work (w = 0). So ΔU = q exactly. All heat goes to internal energy. This is why constant-volume calorimetry is simpler—no work term to worry about.'

slides.title: Enthalpy & Enthalpy Change

points.label: Enthalpy (H)
points.text: H = U + PV. Useful for reactions at constant pressure (most lab reactions).

points.label: Enthalpy change
points.text: ΔH = ΔU + Δ(PV). At constant P: ΔH = ΔU + PΔV = q.

points.label: Why ΔH?
points.text: In a lab, we can't easily control internal energy. But we CAN control pressure (use open beakers). ΔH = heat released/absorbed at constant P.

example.problem: Combustion of CH₄: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = -890 kJ. What does this mean?
example.solution: When 1 mole of methane burns at constant pressure, 890 kJ of heat is RELEASED (negative ΔH = exothermic). This heats your home or kitchen.

slides.inSimpleWords: Enthalpy is the 'heat at constant pressure'—exactly what you measure in a lab. Negative ΔH = heat released. Positive ΔH = heat absorbed.

image.alt: Enthalpy & Enthalpy Change — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Why Enthalpy Matters: Lab Reality
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'We always use open beakers in the lab, not sealed containers. Why measure ΔH instead of ΔU?' Dr. Singh explains: 'In a sealed container, ΔU is hard to measure—you need to know pressure, volume, temperature changes. In an open beaker, pressure is always 1 atm. Heat flows out (or in), that's ΔH. Much simpler.'

image.alt: Why Enthalpy Matters: Lab Reality — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Exothermic vs. Endothermic Reactions

points.label: Exothermic (ΔH < 0)
points.text: Releases heat. Products lower energy than reactants. Examples: combustion, neutralization, respiration.

points.label: Endothermic (ΔH > 0)
points.text: Absorbs heat. Products higher energy than reactants. Examples: melting ice, boiling water, photosynthesis.

points.label: Real-life
points.text: Exothermic reactions are often spontaneous (flame ignites, body burns food). Endothermic reactions need energy input (ice melts only when heated).

example.problem: Melting ice: H₂O(s) → H₂O(l), ΔH = +6.01 kJ/mol. Is this spontaneous at room temperature?
example.solution: ΔH > 0 (endothermic). Alone, NO—ice needs heat input. But at T > 0°C, the entropy gain dominates, and ΔG becomes negative (spontaneous). Disorder (liquid) > order (solid) at higher T.

slides.inSimpleWords: Exothermic = heat out (feels warm). Endothermic = heat in (feels cold). Your hand feels cold when ice melts because it's absorbing heat from your skin.

image.alt: Exothermic vs. Endothermic Reactions — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Instant Noodles: Endothermic Hand Warmer
slides.storyContext: Priya holds a hand-warmer pouch that feels ICE COLD at first, then hot. 'But it absorbs heat from my hand—shouldn't it cool down further?' Dr. Singh explains: 'The pouch contains a chemical reaction that's ENDOTHERMIC but forced to go forward. The reaction absorbs your body heat and... converts it to heat anyway through a different route.'

example.problem: An instant cold pack contains ammonium nitrate. NH₄NO₃(s) → NH₄⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq), ΔH = +25 kJ/mol. You slam it—the salt dissolves. Why does your hand get COLD?
example.solution: The dissolving is endothermic (ΔH > 0). It ABSORBS heat from surroundings (your hand) to break the crystal lattice and hydrate ions. Your hand cools as it donates energy. This is why instant cold packs work—endothermic reactions pull heat away.

slides.inSimpleWords: Endothermic reactions absorb heat from the environment. Cold packs exploit this to chill your hand.

image.alt: Instant Noodles: Endothermic Hand Warmer — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Bond Enthalpy & Energy Diagrams

points.label: Bond enthalpy
points.text: Energy required to break a bond (always positive). ΔH_rxn = Σ(bonds broken) - Σ(bonds formed).

points.label: Energy diagram
points.text: Y-axis: energy. Exothermic curves downward (products lower). Endothermic curves upward (products higher).

points.label: Activation energy
points.text: Minimum energy needed to break reactant bonds and start reaction. Catalyst lowers Ea, not ΔH.

example.problem: H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. Given: H-H = 436 kJ/mol, Cl-Cl = 243 kJ/mol, H-Cl = 431 kJ/mol. Find ΔH.
example.solution: Bonds broken: H-H (436) + Cl-Cl (243) = 679 kJ. Bonds formed: 2 × H-Cl (2 × 431) = 862 kJ. ΔH = 679 - 862 = -183 kJ (exothermic).

slides.inSimpleWords: Breaking bonds costs energy; forming them releases energy. If new bonds release more than old bonds consumed, the reaction is exothermic.

slides.title: Hess's Law: Adding Reactions

points.label: Principle
points.text: ΔH for a reaction depends only on initial & final states, not path. If you add reactions, add their ΔH values.

points.label: Using Hess's Law
points.text: Break a complex reaction into known simple reactions. Add them algebraically.

points.label: Example
points.text: C(s) + CO₂(g) → 2CO(g). If we know: C + O₂ → CO₂ (ΔH₁), 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂ (ΔH₂), we can combine to get the target reaction.

example.problem: Given: (1) C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH₁ = -393 kJ. (2) 2CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g), ΔH₂ = -566 kJ. Find ΔH for: 2C(s) + O₂(g) → 2CO(g).

slides.inSimpleWords: Hess's Law is like adding equations: if you know reaction paths A→B and B→C, you can find ΔH for A→C without running the experiment.

image.alt: Hess's Law: Adding Reactions — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Hess's Law: Routing Around an Obstacle
slides.storyContext: Priya wonders: 'We can measure the heat released when methane burns. But what if we want the enthalpy of a reaction we can't easily run in the lab?'

example.problem: Find ΔH for: C(graphite) → C(diamond). (You can't run this reaction at room temperature—it takes huge pressure.) Use: (1) C(graphite) + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH₁ = -393.5 kJ. (2) C(diamond) + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH₂ = -395.4 kJ.
example.solution: Reverse (2): CO₂ → C(diamond) + O₂, ΔH = +395.4 kJ. Add to (1): [C(graphite) + O₂ → CO₂] + [CO₂ → C(diamond) + O₂] → C(graphite) → C(diamond). ΔH = -393.5 + 395.4 = +1.9 kJ. Diamond formation requires energy input (as expected—diamond is less stable than graphite).

slides.inSimpleWords: Hess's Law lets you find the ΔH of reactions you can't run directly by combining measurements of reactions you can run.

image.alt: Hess's Law: Routing Around an Obstacle — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Spontaneity & Gibbs Free Energy (Intro)

points.label: Spontaneous
points.text: Reaction happens on its own without external energy (but may be very slow)

points.label: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS
points.text: Gibbs free energy. ΔG < 0 = spontaneous, ΔG > 0 = non-spontaneous.

points.label: Role of entropy
points.text: ΔS > 0 (disorder increases) favors spontaneity. At high T, TΔS dominates even if ΔH > 0.

example.problem: Melting ice at 0°C: ΔH = +6.01 kJ/mol, ΔS = +22 J/(mol·K). Is it spontaneous?
example.solution: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS = 6010 J - (273 K)(22 J/K) = 6010 - 6006 ≈ 0. Right at equilibrium. At T > 0°C, TΔS > ΔH, so ΔG < 0 (spontaneous melting).

slides.inSimpleWords: A reaction is spontaneous if ΔG is negative. ΔG weighs enthalpy (energy change) against entropy (disorder change). High temperature favors disorder.

image.alt: Spontaneity & Gibbs Free Energy (Intro) — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Why Some Reactions Are 'Uphill' But Still Happen
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Photosynthesis absorbs energy (ΔH > 0) and creates order from CO₂ (ΔS < 0). Shouldn't it be completely impossible?' Dr. Singh smiles: 'It should be, BUT... the Sun provides free energy. Light drives ΔG negative, even though both ΔH and ΔS are 'bad' alone.'

image.alt: Why Some Reactions Are 'Uphill' But Still Happen — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Worked Problem: Hess's Law in Practice
slides.storyContext: Dr. Singh assigns a calorimetry lab. Priya must find the heat of formation of NO using Hess's Law.

example.problem: Find ΔH for: N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g), given: (1) 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ (ΔH₁ = -114 kJ), (2) N₂ + 2O₂ → 2NO₂ (ΔH₂, provided from data).
example.solution: Given (1): 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂, ΔH₁ = -114 kJ. Reverse it: 2NO₂ → 2NO + O₂, ΔH = +114 kJ. If (2) gives ΔH₂ for N₂ + 2O₂ → 2NO₂, add them: [N₂ + 2O₂ → 2NO₂] + [2NO₂ → 2NO + O₂] → N₂ + O₂ → 2NO. ΔH(target) = ΔH₂ + 114. Typically ΔH₂ ≈ -66 kJ, so ΔH ≈ +180 kJ (endothermic).

slides.inSimpleWords: Hess's Law lets you calculate ΔH for reactions you can't directly measure by combining known reactions.

image.alt: Worked Problem: Hess's Law in Practice — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Entropy: The Universe's Preference for Chaos
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Why does disorder matter?' Dr. Singh explains: 'Entropy (ΔS) measures disorder. At high temperature, disorder wins. This is why ice melts, why perfume evaporates, why everything mixes. The second law says the universe ALWAYS increases entropy. Life is a local bubble of order, but we pay for it by dumping heat and waste to surroundings.'

slides.title: Why Fire Never Reverses: Entropy Arrow
slides.storyContext: Priya observes: 'When a candle burns, it releases heat and CO₂ gas. But we never see CO₂ spontaneously reform into candle wax and heat—even though it's theoretically possible. Why?' Dr. Singh smiles: 'Entropy. Burning increases disorder (solid → gas, concentrated heat → dispersed). The reverse would require the universe to spontaneously decrease entropy—thermodynamically forbidden by the Second Law.'

slides.title: Why Reactions Slow Down: Activation Energy & Kinetics

points.label: Activation energy (Ea)
points.text: Minimum energy to break reactant bonds and start reaction. Even exothermic reactions (ΔH < 0) need Ea to get going.

points.label: Kinetics
points.text: Studies how FAST reactions occur. ΔH tells you IF a reaction goes, but Ea tells you HOW FAST.

points.label: Catalyst
points.text: Lowers Ea without changing ΔH. Speeds reaction without changing final products or energy released.

example.problem: Diamond and graphite: both carbon. Diamond is higher energy (ΔH > 0). Why don't diamonds spontaneously turn to graphite?
example.solution: ΔH > 0 (unfavorable), but Ea is HUGE. Converting a carbon lattice requires breaking many C-C bonds simultaneously—impossible at room temperature. Kinetics, not thermodynamics, protects your diamonds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Even if a reaction is thermodynamically favorable (ΔG < 0), it might not happen because the activation energy is too high. Kinetics controls speed; thermodynamics controls direction.

slides.title: Why Doesn't Ice Spontaneously Form at Room Temperature?
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Ice melts at 0°C. So at 25°C, shouldn't water spontaneously freeze since that's lower energy?'

example.problem: Freezing water at 25°C: ΔH = -6.01 kJ/mol (releases heat), but ΔS = -22 J/(mol·K) (disorder decreases). Why isn't this spontaneous?
example.solution: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS = -6010 - (298 K)(-22 J/K) = -6010 + 6556 = +546 J > 0. Non-spontaneous because the entropy penalty dominates at 298 K. Nature prefers disorder (liquid) over order (ice) at room temperature.

image.alt: Why Doesn't Ice Spontaneously Form at Room Temperature? — Thermodynamics

slides.title: Thermodynamics Essentials

points.text: Internal energy (U) = total energy of particles; changes via heat (q) and work (w)
First Law: ΔU = q + w (energy conserved)
Enthalpy (H): ΔH = heat at constant pressure (lab reactions)
Exothermic: ΔH < 0 (releases heat). Endothermic: ΔH > 0 (absorbs heat)
Hess's Law: ΔH depends on initial & final states, not path
Spontaneity: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS. Low ΔG = spontaneous (likely to happen)

slides.inSimpleWords: Thermodynamics explains WHY reactions happen and HOW MUCH energy changes. Energy is conserved. Spontaneous reactions have ΔG < 0, favored by low enthalpy and high entropy.

image.alt: Thermodynamics Essentials — Thermodynamics

subject: Chemistry
title: Balance of Power: Chemical Equilibrium
hook: Why doesn't every reaction go to completion? The answer is equilibrium—a dynamic battle between forward and reverse reactions.

slides.title: Equilibrium
slides.storyContext: Dr. Kumar pours colorless nitrogen dioxide gas into a sealed bottle. Suddenly, it turns brown (N₂O₄). After a while, the color stabilizes. 'It looks done. But it's not. Both reactions are happening, forever.'

image.alt: Equilibrium — Equilibrium

slides.title: Reversible Reactions & Dynamic Equilibrium
slides.storyContext: Most reactions are reversible: A + B ⇌ C + D. At first, forward dominates. Gradually, reverse catches up. When rates match, EQUILIBRIUM is reached—no net change, but both reactions continue. This is dynamic equilibrium.

image.alt: Reversible Reactions & Dynamic Equilibrium — Equilibrium

slides.title: The Brown Gas Colour Shift
slides.storyContext: Priya watches the sealed bottle carefully. 'The colour is getting darker, but slower. Is the reaction stopping?' Dr. Kumar explains: 'NO₂ is combining into N₂O₄ (colourless dimer). But N₂O₄ is also splitting back into NO₂. At first, combining is faster (more NO₂ molecules). As they dimerise, NO₂ concentration drops, so combining slows. Meanwhile, splitting speeds up. When the rates match—equilibrium. The bottle looks stable, but both reactions continue invisibly.'

image.alt: The Brown Gas Colour Shift — Equilibrium

slides.title: Equilibrium Constant (Kc & Kp)

points.label: Definition
points.text: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD at constant T: Kc = [C]^c [D]^d / [A]^a [B]^b at equilibrium.

points.label: K > 1
points.text: Products favored (equilibrium shifts right)

points.label: K < 1
points.text: Reactants favored (equilibrium shifts left)

points.label: K for gases
points.text: Kp uses partial pressures instead of concentrations

example.problem: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. At equilibrium: [N₂] = 1 M, [H₂] = 3 M, [NH₃] = 2 M. Find Kc.
example.solution: Kc = [NH₃]² / ([N₂][H₂]³) = (2)² / (1)(3)³ = 4 / 27 ≈ 0.148. K < 1, so reactants (N₂, H₂) are favored; ammonia synthesis is not efficient without pressure/temperature control.

slides.inSimpleWords: The equilibrium constant K measures whether products or reactants are favored. Large K = products win. Small K = reactants win.

image.alt: Equilibrium Constant (Kc & Kp) — Equilibrium

slides.title: Computing K: The Ammonia Factory
slides.storyContext: Priya calculates K for the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃) at different temperatures. At 300 K, K is huge (products dominate). At 500 K, K drops 1000-fold (reactants start winning).

example.problem: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. At 300 K, Kc = 6.9×10⁸. At 500 K, Kc = 1.7×10⁻³. What does this tell you?
example.solution: At 300 K: K >> 1. Equilibrium heavily favors products (lots of NH₃). BUT the reaction is too slow—you can't wait 100 years. At 500 K: K << 1. Most N₂ and H₂ remain unreacted—not useful. Industrial process uses ~450 K (compromise: K ≈ 1.5, AND reaction is fast enough to be practical).

slides.inSimpleWords: A large K is good (products), but if the reaction is too slow, nothing happens. Real chemistry balances yield (K) with rate (kinetics).

image.alt: Computing K: The Ammonia Factory — Equilibrium

slides.title: Why K Is Always Positive (Always)
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Can K be negative?' Dr. Kumar laughs: 'No. K is a ratio of concentrations raised to powers. All concentrations are positive. So K is always positive. But K CAN be very small (< 1) or very large (> 1).'

slides.title: Le Chatelier's Principle: Disturbing Equilibrium

points.label: Principle
points.text: When you disturb an equilibrium system, it responds to undo the change.

points.label: Changes
points.text: (1) Concentration: add reactant → shift right (forward). (2) Pressure (gas): increase total P → shift toward fewer moles. (3) Temperature: add heat → shift in endothermic direction.

points.label: Catalyst
points.text: Speeds up both forward & reverse equally → NO shift in equilibrium position.

example.problem: N₂O₄(g, colorless) ⇌ 2NO₂(g, brown). You cool the sealed bottle. Which way does it shift?
example.solution: N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ is endothermic (takes heat to split). Cooling favors the reverse. Equilibrium shifts LEFT (toward N₂O₄, colorless). Bottle pales.

slides.inSimpleWords: Le Chatelier's Principle: if you stress an equilibrium (add reactant, heat, increase pressure), the system fights back by shifting to oppose the stress.

image.alt: Le Chatelier's Principle: Disturbing Equilibrium — Equilibrium

slides.title: The System Fights Back
slides.storyContext: Dr. Kumar performs a live demo: sealed bottle containing N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ (colorless ⇌ brown). He adds ice around the bottle. 'Watch closely.' The brown color fades. 'Equilibrium shifted LEFT. The system 'wanted' to stay in equilibrium, so cooling (removing heat) made it reassociate the NO₂ into N₂O₄.'

image.alt: The System Fights Back — Equilibrium

slides.title: Effect of Concentration Changes

points.label: Add reactant
points.text: Equilibrium shifts right (forward) to use up the extra.

points.label: Remove product
points.text: Equilibrium shifts right to make more product.

points.label: Add inert gas at constant V
points.text: No effect (partial pressures of reactants/products unchanged).

points.label: Example: Haber process
points.text: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. Industrially, remove NH₃ as it forms (condense it) → forces equilibrium right, improves yield.

example.problem: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI. At equilibrium, you inject more H₂. Qualitatively, what happens?
example.solution: Equilibrium shifts RIGHT to consume the extra H₂ and produce more HI. New equilibrium has higher [HI] and [I₂], but [H₂] is restored partially (but still higher than before).

slides.inSimpleWords: Adding more of a reactant pushes the reaction forward. Removing product does the same. This is how industrial chemists maximize output.

image.alt: Effect of Concentration Changes — Equilibrium

slides.title: Product Removal: The Dairy Strategy
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'In cheese-making, they remove moisture and lactose. Does that shift the fermentation equilibrium?' Dr. Kumar smiles: 'Exactly. Removing lactose (product of the microbial reaction) drives the equilibrium forward—more lactose is consumed to maintain balance.'

example.problem: In fermentation: sugar ⇌ ethanol + CO₂. If you remove ethanol (distillation), does the reaction 'want' to produce more ethanol?
example.solution: Yes. Le Chatelier: removing product shifts equilibrium right (forward), favoring more ethanol production. This is why distillers actively remove ethanol—it pushes equilibrium and maximizes final yield.

slides.inSimpleWords: Remove products to force the reaction forward. This is used everywhere: cheese-making, distilleries, drug manufacturing.

image.alt: Product Removal: The Dairy Strategy — Equilibrium

slides.title: Effect of Pressure & Volume

points.label: Increasing pressure (decrease volume)
points.text: Shifts equilibrium toward side with FEWER gas moles.

points.label: Example: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃
points.text: Left: 4 moles (1 N₂ + 3 H₂). Right: 2 moles (2 NH₃). High pressure shifts RIGHT (fewer moles = fewer molecules = lower pressure).

points.label: Industrial
points.text: Haber process runs at ~200-400 atm to shift equilibrium right and maximize NH₃.

example.problem: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g). You compress the gas at constant T. Which direction does it shift?
example.solution: Left: 2 moles. Right: 1 mole. High pressure favors fewer moles → shifts RIGHT (forms more N₂O₄). Color fades from brown (NO₂) to colorless (N₂O₄).

slides.inSimpleWords: High pressure favors reactions that produce fewer gas molecules. This is a key strategy in industrial chemistry to boost yields.

image.alt: Effect of Pressure & Volume — Equilibrium

slides.title: Crushing the Gas into Product
slides.storyContext: Arjun wonders: 'Why does high pressure help ammonia production?' Dr. Kumar illustrates: 'Imagine 4 gas molecules (N₂ + 3H₂) bumping around in a container. High pressure squeezes them closer. Collisions become more frequent. And they combine into 2 NH₃ molecules—fewer total. The system 'chooses' fewer moles to relieve the pressure stress.'

image.alt: Crushing the Gas into Product — Equilibrium

slides.title: Effect of Temperature

points.label: Exothermic reaction (ΔH < 0)
points.text: Heat is a product. Increase T → shifts LEFT (reverse). Decrease T → shifts RIGHT (forward, yields increase).

points.label: Endothermic reaction (ΔH > 0)
points.text: Heat is a reactant. Increase T → shifts RIGHT (forward). Decrease T → shifts LEFT.

points.label: Temperature also changes K
points.text: Pressure/concentration DON'T change K. But T always changes K (changes equilibrium position & magnitude).

example.problem: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = -92 kJ (exothermic). For maximum NH₃ yield, should you increase or decrease temperature?
example.solution: Exothermic → heat is a product. Low T shifts equilibrium RIGHT, maximizing NH₃. But low T also slows the reaction (kinetics). Haber uses ~450°C (compromise: acceptable rate + decent yield).

slides.inSimpleWords: For exothermic reactions, cooling pushes equilibrium forward (products). But you lose reaction speed. Industrial chemistry is a balance.

image.alt: Effect of Temperature — Equilibrium

slides.title: The Haber Dilemma: Speed vs. Yield
slides.storyContext: Priya studies the Haber process data. At 300 K, K ≈ 10⁹ (99% NH₃). At 500 K, K ≈ 10⁻³ (99% N₂ + H₂). At 450 K, K ≈ 1.5 (only 30% NH₃). 'Shouldn't we just use 300 K?' she asks. Dr. Kumar explains: 'At 300 K, the reaction is too slow—it would take decades. At 450 K, it's fast enough AND yield is acceptable. This compromise is why the Haber process was possible—and why it changed civilization.'

example.problem: Haber process at different temperatures: 300 K (K huge, reaction dead slow), 450 K (K = 1.5, fast enough), 600 K (K tiny, mostly reactants). Why use 450 K?
example.solution: At 450 K: equilibrium is not ideal (only 30-50% NH₃ depending on pressure), BUT combined with 200+ atm pressure and product removal, it's viable. More importantly, the reaction runs at industrial timescale (hours, not decades). This balance enabled the Haber process—feeding billions of people.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real chemistry isn't just about thermodynamics (ΔG < 0). It's about kinetics too (rate). You often sacrifice some yield for speed.

image.alt: The Haber Dilemma: Speed vs. Yield — Equilibrium

slides.title: Worked Problem: Multi-factor Equilibrium
slides.storyContext: Dr. Kumar assigns a real-world scenario: maximizing acetylene production from calcium carbide (CaC₂ + H₂O ⇌ C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂).

example.problem: To maximize acetylene yield, should you: (A) increase T, (B) decrease T, (C) remove C₂H₂ as it forms? Assume reaction is exothermic.
example.solution: (B) & (C) are both correct strategies. (B) Low T favors products (exothermic). (C) Removing product forces equilibrium forward (Le Chatelier). Industrially, both are used: water is supplied continuously (removes CaC₂ as it reacts, removes H₂O, shifts forward), and cooling jackets keep T moderate. This drives reaction completion.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real industrial chemistry uses multiple Le Chatelier strategies at once: remove products, adjust temperature, optimize pressure—to maximize output.

image.alt: Worked Problem: Multi-factor Equilibrium — Equilibrium

slides.title: Ionic Equilibria: Kw & pH

points.label: Water ionization
points.text: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻. Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C.

points.label: pH definition
points.text: pH = -log[H⁺]. Neutral: pH 7. Acidic: pH < 7. Basic: pH > 7.

points.label: pOH
points.text: pOH = -log[OH⁻]. pH + pOH = 14 at 25°C.

example.problem: A solution has [H⁺] = 10⁻³ M. Find pH and [OH⁻].

slides.inSimpleWords: Water itself ionizes slightly, creating H⁺ and OH⁻ ions. The product [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴ always. pH measures the acidity (H⁺ concentration).

image.alt: Ionic Equilibria: Kw & pH — Equilibrium

slides.title: The pH Scale: Logarithmic Common Sense
slides.storyContext: Priya struggles: 'Why is pH logarithmic instead of just H⁺ concentration?' Dr. Kumar explains: 'Because life operates over a 10-billionfold range of H⁺. A linear scale would go from 0 to 10,000,000,000. Logarithmic compresses it to 0-14, so we can see both strong acid (pH 0) and strong base (pH 14) on one scale. Pretty clever.'

image.alt: The pH Scale: Logarithmic Common Sense — Equilibrium

slides.title: Buffers: Resisting pH Change
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Why doesn't pure water's pH change when you add a tiny bit of acid?' Dr. Kumar explains: 'In pure water, [H⁺] = 10⁻⁷. Adding acid from a weak source (e.g., a single drop of HCl in a liter) might add 10⁻⁸ M. That's only a 10% change—barely moves pH. But a buffer (like acetic acid + acetate) actively resists change—it can absorb added acid/base without pH shift. Life depends on buffers.'

slides.title: Solubility Equilibria & Ksp

points.label: Solubility product (Ksp)
points.text: For salt AB: AB(s) ⇌ A⁺(aq) + B⁻(aq). Ksp = [A⁺][B⁻]. Smaller Ksp = less soluble.

points.label: Predicting precipitation
points.text: If [A⁺][B⁻] > Ksp, salt precipitates. If < Ksp, it dissolves.

points.label: Common ion effect
points.text: Adding A⁺ or B⁻ shifts equilibrium left (Le Chatelier), reducing solubility of AB.

example.problem: AgCl has Ksp = 1.8×10⁻¹⁰. If [Ag⁺] = 10⁻⁵ M, what [Cl⁻] causes precipitation?
example.solution: At equilibrium: [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] = Ksp. (10⁻⁵)[Cl⁻] = 1.8×10⁻¹⁰. [Cl⁻] = 1.8×10⁻⁵ M. If [Cl⁻] > 1.8×10⁻⁵ M, AgCl precipitates.

slides.inSimpleWords: Salts dissolve in water until equilibrium is reached (Ksp). Add more of an ion, and the salt precipitates out—common ion effect.

slides.title: Common Ion Effect: Reducing Solubility
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'If I add NaCl to a saturated NaCl solution, what happens?' Dr. Kumar explains: 'NaCl is already at maximum solubility. Adding Cl⁻ (common ion) shifts the equilibrium left. Sodium chloride precipitates out. This is how we 'salt out' crystals.'

example.problem: A solution is saturated with NaCl. Adding NaCl (concentration already 6 M) causes crystallization. Why?
example.solution: NaCl(s) ⇌ Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), Ksp = 36. At equilibrium [Na⁺][Cl⁻] = 36. Adding Cl⁻ makes [Cl⁻] > equilibrium value. System shifts left to restore Ksp, precipitating solid NaCl.

slides.inSimpleWords: Adding an ion shifts the solubility equilibrium (Le Chatelier). Use this to crystallize salts or remove ions from solution.

slides.title: Weak Acids & Bases: Not Quite Equilibrium
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'Why is HCl strong but acetic acid weak?' Dr. Kumar explains: 'HCl completely dissociates: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻ (100%). Acetic acid only partially: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ (~1%). Most acetic acid stays molecular. Equilibrium favors the undissociated form.'

slides.title: Ka & Kb: Acid & Base Strength

points.label: Acid dissociation constant (Ka)
points.text: HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻. Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. Larger Ka = stronger acid (dissociates more).

points.label: Base dissociation constant (Kb)
points.text: B + H₂O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻. Kb = [BH⁺][OH⁻]/[B]. Larger Kb = stronger base.

points.label: Relationship
points.text: Ka × Kb = Kw (= 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C). Weak acid pairs with strong conjugate base.

example.problem: Acetic acid: Ka = 1.8×10⁻⁵. What's the pH of 0.1 M acetic acid?
example.solution: At equilibrium: Ka = [H⁺][CH₃COO⁻]/[CH₃COOH] = 1.8×10⁻⁵. Assume x = [H⁺]. Then (x)(x)/(0.1-x) ≈ (x²)/(0.1) = 1.8×10⁻⁵. x² = 1.8×10⁻⁶. x = 1.3×10⁻³ M. pH = -log(1.3×10⁻³) ≈ 2.9.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ka measures acid strength; Kb measures base strength. Larger values mean stronger dissociation and lower pH (for acids).

slides.title: Acid-Base Pairs: The Conjugate Connection
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks: 'If acetic acid is weak, is acetate ion strong?' Dr. Kumar nods: 'Exactly. In water, acetate steals H⁺ from H₂O, making it a weak base. Weak acid + strong conjugate base. Strong acid + weak conjugate base. This partnership comes from Ka × Kb = Kw.'

slides.title: pH Calculation: Weak Acid Challenge
slides.storyContext: Priya calculates the pH of a weak acid solution using the equilibrium expression and approximations.

example.problem: Hypochlorous acid (HOCl) has Ka = 3.0×10⁻⁸. Find pH of 0.05 M HOCl.
example.solution: HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻. Ka = [H⁺][OCl⁻]/[HOCl] = 3.0×10⁻⁸. Let x = [H⁺]. (x²)/(0.05-x) ≈ (x²)/(0.05) = 3.0×10⁻⁸. x² = 1.5×10⁻⁹. x = [H⁺] = 3.9×10⁻⁵ M. pH = -log(3.9×10⁻⁵) ≈ 4.4. Verify: Ka is small, so approximation valid (x << 0.05).

slides.inSimpleWords: Weak acids only partially dissociate. Set up the equilibrium expression, assume x << initial concentration, solve for [H⁺], then pH.

slides.title: Design an Industrial Process
slides.storyContext: You're an engineer at a fertilizer plant. You need to maximize ammonia production. What conditions would you recommend?

example.problem: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = -92 kJ, K increases with lower T. Recommend: (1) Temperature, (2) Pressure, (3) Concentration management.
example.solution: (1) T: ≈450°C (low enough for good K, high enough for acceptable rate). (2) P: 200-400 atm (shifts toward NH₃, 2 moles < 4 moles). (3) Remove NH₃ as it forms (condense the liquid). This is the Haber process used worldwide—feeding billions.

image.alt: Design an Industrial Process — Equilibrium

slides.title: Equilibrium Mastery

points.text: Equilibrium constant K measures product vs. reactant favorability; depends on T only
Le Chatelier's Principle: system opposes stress (concentration, pressure, T)
Concentration changes: add reactant → shift forward; remove product → shift forward
Pressure (gas): high P → shifts toward fewer moles
Temperature: for exothermic, low T shifts forward; also decreases K
Ionic equilibrium: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 10⁻¹⁴; pH = -log[H⁺]

slides.inSimpleWords: Equilibrium is not 'done'—it's a dynamic balance where forward and reverse reactions continue at the same rate. Le Chatelier's Principle lets you manipulate equilibrium for practical gains.

image.alt: Equilibrium Mastery — Equilibrium
